paper_context.research_question: Can carefully enhanced sequential LSTM-based architectures, possibly combined with syntactic (tree-LSTM) modeling, improve state-of-the-art performance on the SNLI natural language inference benchmark?
main_claims: A carefully designed enhanced sequential inference model (ESIM) based on BiLSTMs, attention, local inference enhancement (difference and element-wise product), and average+max pooling outperforms prior published models on SNLI, achieving 88.0% accuracy.
Incorporating syntactic parsing via tree-LSTMs and ensembling with ESIM (Hybrid Inference Model, HIM) yields further improvement and reaches a new reported state-of-the-art accuracy of 88.6% on SNLI.

Key components that materially contribute to performance include: bidirectional LSTM encodings for input and composition, the specific soft-attention alignment over contextualized hidden states, the enhancement operations (difference and product), and average+max pooling; removing or altering these degrades accuracy significantly.
Sequential chain LSTM approaches still have untapped potential for NLI and can serve as strong baselines before resorting to more complex architectures.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Held-out accuracy on SNLI test set (comparative to prior work)
Ablation studies measuring impact of individual components (e.g., BiLSTM vs MLP, diff/prod features, pooling choices, tree-LSTM inclusion)
Statistical significance of performance differences across model variants
Model size and parameter count vs performance (efficiency/complexity trade-offs)
Qualitative analyses of attention and gate activations to illustrate when tree vs sequential models differ
Reproducibility details (training hyperparameters, embeddings, parser used, code release)

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that a carefully engineered sequential BiLSTM-based architecture (ESIM) with attention over contextualized hidden states, local inference enhancement (concatenation of vectors, their difference and element-wise product), BiLSTM-based inference composition, and average+max pooling attains new top SNLI performance (88.0%). It then argues that adding syntactic tree-LSTM encodings and ensembling with ESIM (HIM) yields further gains (88.6%). The empirical backbone is comparative test accuracy reporting and ablation experiments claiming statistical significance. The reasoning chain is: (i) BiLSTM contextual encodings + attention produce better alignments than bag-of-embeddings/decomposable approaches; (ii) enhancing local aligned pairs with diff/prod and feeding through BiLSTM composition yields strong single-model performance; (iii) pooling via avg+max is preferable to summation; (iv) syntactic tree-LSTMs capture complementary constituency-level signals that, when ensembled, further improve accuracy. Strength of argument rests on numerical improvements (0.6% ensemble gain, several ablation deltas up to ~4%) and targeted ablations. Weaknesses in the reasoning chain arise from reliance on published baselines for comparison (possible preprocessing or hyperparameter mismatch), limited reporting of experimental variance (number of runs, seeds), modest absolute improvement from syntax (0.6%), and ensembling choice conflating complementary signal with simple variance reduction. Qualitative interpretability evidence is anecdotal (single example). Overall logical flow is coherent but some inferential steps (e.g., superiority of BiLSTM-attention over decomposable attention, and causal role of tree-LSTM beyond ensemble effects) are under-supported by controlled, same-pipeline comparisons and variance estimates.

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If baseline reproductions under identical preprocessing confirm ESIM's 88.0% mean with low variance, the claim that sequential architectures suffice is upheld.
If multiple random seeds show small variance (<0.3%) then the reported ablation deltas (>=0.9%) are meaningful; otherwise differences may be within sampling noise.

If standalone tree-LSTM (same pipeline) improves single-model performance or systematic per-example analysis shows tree-LSTM correcting ESIM errors, then syntactic contribution is verified beyond ensemble variance reduction.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes ESIM, an enhanced sequential BiLSTM-based model for Natural Language Inference (NLI) that combines BiLSTM input encoding and composition, soft attention over contextualized hidden states, local enhancement via concatenation of hidden, attended, difference and element-wise product vectors, and average+max pooling; ESIM is reported at 88.0% accuracy on SNLI. The authors further ensemble ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM model (HIM) by averaging predicted probabilities, yielding 88.6% accuracy. Ablations attribute substantial contribution to BiLSTM encodings (vs MLP), the diff/prod enhancement, and average+max pooling (vs summation). The paper argues sequential models retain untapped potential and that syntactic parse-based tree-LSTMs complement ESIM. Methodologically, the paper gives a clear model design and training recipe (optimizer, lr, dropout, embeddings), reports single train/dev/test accuracies and some ablation comparisons with t-test claims. Missing or weak evidence areas include limited reporting of experimental variance (number of runs, seeds), incomplete hyperparameter/early-stopping detail, reliance on published baselines without controlled re-runs under the same preprocessing, and the ensemble nature of the syntactic gain (no single-model tree-LSTM standalone performance reported clearly). Key assumptions (fair comparability to prior work, parser quality, statistical-test validity) must hold for claims to be robust.
logical_argument_graph: P1: BiLSTM contextualized encodings capture word + context better than bag-of-embeddings or MLP mappings (supported by heldout comparisons).
P2: Soft-attention over BiLSTM hidden states yields better local alignments than decomposable (bag) attention, enabling improved local inference modeling.
P3: Enhancing aligned local vectors with concatenation of original, attended, difference and elementwise product highlights relational signals (e.g., contradiction) improving downstream inference.
P4: Composing enhanced local inference via BiLSTM (or tree-LSTM) and pooling (average+max) forms a fixed-length representation that leads to strong classification.
P5: ESIM architecture combining P1-P4 attains 88.0% test accuracy on SNLI, exceeding published baselines (evidence: Table 1).
P6: Adding a syntactic tree-LSTM and ensembling with ESIM yields additional 0.6% absolute gain to 88.6% (HIM), indicating parse-based structure complements sequential model.
C: Therefore, carefully designed sequential LSTM-based models, possibly combined with parse-aware tree-LSTMs, can set new SOTA on SNLI and serve as strong baselines.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that careful architectural choices applied to sequential BiLSTM-based NLI models (ESIM) — specifically: contextualized BiLSTM encodings, soft attention computed over those contextualized hidden states, explicit local enhancement (concatenate [h; h_att; h-h_att; h * h_att]), BiLSTM-based inference composition, and average+max pooling — produce substantial performance improvements on SNLI, surpassing prior published results (ESIM 88.0%). The authors then ensemble ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM model (trained on Stanford PCFG parses) to form HIM, which yields a modest further gain (88.6%). The paper supports these claims with comparative test accuracies, focused ablations that isolate pooling, enhancement features, and use of BiLSTM vs MLP, and an interpretability anecdote (gate norms / attention visualization) suggesting syntactic nodes sometimes provide complementary signals. The manuscript positions itself relative to decomposable attention (Parikh et al.) and prior complex sequential/tree hybrids (Munkhdalai & Yu), claiming that sequential chain models still hold untapped potential when carefully designed. Overall, the contribution is an engineering-methodological refinement: not a brand-new paradigm, but a compact, well-justified set of design choices plus ablation evidence showing they matter empirically on SNLI.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Prior SOTA includes decomposable attention and several complex sequential/tree hybrids (Parikh et al.; Munkhdalai & Yu).
L2: Contextualized BiLSTM hidden states better capture word-in-context semantics than raw embeddings used in some decomposable attention variants.
L3: Computing soft attention directly over contextualized BiLSTM/tree-LSTM states yields stronger local alignments (eij = ā_i^T b̄_j).
L4: Enhancing aligned pairs via concatenation of (h; h_att; h-h_att; h * h_att) sharpens local inference signals useful for classification.
L5: Composing enhanced local inference with another BiLSTM (inference composition) and then pooling via average+max yields better sentence-pair representations than simple sum pooling.
L6: ESIM (combining L2-L5) reaches 88.0% on SNLI, outperforming prior published models (empirical evidence Table 1).
L7: Syntactic tree-LSTM encodings capture phrase-level signals that sometimes differ from sequential attention and can be complementary.
L8: Ensembling ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM (HIM) gives marginal additional improvement to 88.6% (Table 1), indicating complementarity.
L9: Ablations (pooling, enhancement ops, replacing BiLSTMs with MLPs) show large drops, supporting claims that specific components materially contribute.
L10: Therefore, carefully enhanced sequential chain LSTM architectures are still strong baselines and syntax-aware components can add modest gains.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes ESIM, a carefully engineered sequential NLI architecture built from BiLSTM input encoders, soft attention over contextualized BiLSTM states, a local inference enhancement step (concatenating representations, their difference, and element-wise product), a BiLSTM inference-composition layer, and average+max pooling into an MLP classifier. ESIM (single model) is reported at 88.0% on SNLI, surpassing previously published numbers. The authors then ensemble ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM model (HIM) by averaging predicted probabilities and report a modest further gain to 88.6%. The paper's argument is: (1) high-quality contextualized BiLSTM encodings + attention yield strong alignments; (2) explicit local enhancement operations (diff, prod) make alignment signals more discriminative; (3) BiLSTM composition and average+max pooling produce more robust fixed-length representations than summation; (4) syntactic tree-LSTM provides complementary signals when ensembled with ESIM. Evidence is primarily held-out/train/test accuracy numbers and an ablation table showing single-variable changes (pooling, removal of diff/prod, replacing BiLSTMs with MLPs) with reported t-test significance (p<0.01). The paper claims reproducibility (code release) but critical details (random seeds, full hyperparameter sweep info, link redacted) are incomplete. The empirical gains are real within the paper's controlled experiments but modest in absolute size (≤0.6% ensemble gain) and sensitive to experimental assumptions (preprocessing, parser quality, single-seed reporting).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript claims that a carefully engineered sequential BiLSTM-based architecture (ESIM)—combining BiLSTM input encoding, attention over contextualized hidden states, local enhancement (concatenate: hidden, attended, diff, element-wise product), BiLSTM inference composition, and average+max pooling—achieves 88.0% on SNLI and outperforms previously published models. Further, ensembling ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM (HIM) by averaging predicted probabilities yields 88.6%. The paper supports these claims with comparative test accuracies (Table 1) and ablations (Table 2) that remove or alter components (pooling, diff/prod, replacing BiLSTM with MLP) and report statistically significant drops (t-test p<0.01). Key evidence is internal: single-run train/dev/test numbers, parameter counts, and focused ablations showing deltas up to ~4%. However, cross-paper comparisons rely on published baseline numbers (possible preprocessing/hyperparameter mismatch). Ablation significance statements lack per-run variance and seed counts, and the syntactic gain primarily arises via ensembling rather than demonstrating clear single-model additive effect. Qualitative interpretability is illustrated via a single case visualization. Overall: the paper reconstructs a coherent argument that particular architectural choices materially improve SNLI performance; the internal ablation evidence supports many component-level claims but external-comparative and statistical robustness claims are partially supported and warrant additional controlled experiments and reporting to reduce uncertainty.

If enhanced local pairs are composed with BiLSTM (inference composition) and pooled with avg+max, then fixed-length representations are more robust than simple summation (Premise: composition+pooling yields improved final classifier inputs).
Therefore, the ESIM architecture (composition of above components) attains superior single-model performance (evidence: ESIM 88.0% on SNLI vs published baselines).

If tree-LSTM captures constituency-level syntactic signals complementary to sequential BiLSTM and ensembling averages predictions, then combining ESIM with tree-LSTM (HIM) increases accuracy (evidence: HIM 88.6%).

Ablation experiments where components are removed/replaced show substantial drops, so component-level claims (importance of BiLSTM encodings, diff/prod, avg+max pooling) are supported internally (evidence: Table 2 deltas).
However, cross-system claims comparing to prior published numbers assume consistent preprocessing/evaluation and statistical significance that are not fully validated (uncertainty nodes).

consensus_findings: The paper presents a clearly specified, modular architecture (ESIM) combining BiLSTM input encoders, attention over contextualized hidden states, local enhancement (concatenate, difference, elementwise product), BiLSTM-based inference composition, and average+max pooling.
Within the authors' experimental pipeline, ESIM attains strong SNLI performance (reported 88.0%) and an ensemble with a syntactic tree-LSTM (HIM) yields a modest additional gain (reported 88.6%).
Authors ran targeted ablation experiments showing that individual components (BiLSTM encoders/composition, diff/prod enhancement, and avg+max pooling) materially affect performance in their setup.
The contribution is primarily an engineering/empirical one: an effective recombination and tuning of known components producing a strong practical baseline for NLI.
Reproducibility intent is signaled (training hyperparameters partially reported and a code release promised).
disagreements: Magnitude and robustness of cross-paper SOTA claim: several reviewers flagged that comparing to published numbers (Table 1) without re-running baselines under the same preprocessing/training pipeline may overstate superiority; others accepted the claim contingent on reproducibility. This is a controlled disagreement about external comparative validity rather than about internal consistency.

Role and value of syntactic tree-LSTM: reviewers agree an ensemble (HIM) improves reported accuracy, but they disagree on whether this indicates substantive complementary syntactic signal (some view it as ensemble/variance reduction) or genuine syntactic complementarity; isolation of standalone tree-LSTM effects is disputed.

Novelty framing: some reviewers characterize the work as a meaningful incremental engineering advance (practically valuable baseline), while others emphasize that novelty is limited because components are largely established; disagreement centers on whether the recombination warrants strong novelty claims.
uncertainty_hotspots: Cross-model comparison validity: reliance on published baseline numbers (possible preprocessing, tokenization, embedding-handling, or evaluation differences) creates uncertainty whether the reported ESIM/HIM gains over prior work hold under identical pipelines (Assumption A1).

Statistical robustness: the paper states t-test significance (p<0.01) but does not report number of independent runs, random seeds, per-run scores, or standard deviations; uncertainty exists whether reported single-number deltas (some small) are robust to random initialization and training variability (Assumption A6).

Syntactic contribution isolation: the tree-LSTM's contribution is primarily reported via ensembling (average probabilities). It is unclear how much of the HIM gain stems from complementary modeling versus variance reduction or ensembling artifacts; standalone tree-LSTM performance and alternative fusion strategies are underreported (Assumptions A2, A4).

Reproducibility details: missing or redacted elements (number of epochs, early stopping, random seeds, full training scripts, redacted code link) impede exact reproduction and raise uncertainty about whether reported numbers will replicate (Assumption A3).

Interpretability generality: qualitative evidence (attention/gate visualization) is anecdotal (single example); uncertainty remains about how frequently the illustrated phenomena occur and whether gate/attention norms reliably explain decisions (Assumption A8).
model_diversity_effects: Ensembling ESIM (sequential, contextualized BiLSTM-based) with a tree-LSTM model produced a modest reported accuracy increase (0.6%). Multiple reviewers interpret this ensemble gain differently: as evidence that syntax captures complementary phrase-level signals in some examples, and alternatively as an expected ensemble variance-reduction effect when combining diverse models.

Diversity of modeling inductive biases (sequence-contextualization vs constituency-structured representations) plausibly yields non-overlapping error modes; the paper presents an anecdotal example consistent with that view but lacks systematic per-example attribution to quantify the effect.

Because the ensemble method used (simple averaging of probabilities) is straightforward, it likely captures model diversity benefits with low implementation complexity, but the lack of other fusion or joint-training experiments leaves open how diversity vs model quality trade off in generating the reported lift.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Prioritize requests that reduce the principal sources of epistemic uncertainty before treating cross-paper superiority claims as settled. Specifically: (1) ask authors to provide reproducible experiments re-running a small set of key competing baselines (e.g., decomposable attention; prominent prior LSTM/tree hybrids) under the exact preprocessing and training pipeline used here, or clearly document any differences in preprocessing that could affect comparability; (2) require reporting of results averaged over multiple independent runs (recommendation: >=5 seeds) with means and standard deviations and clear specification of statistical tests (paired/unpaired), or replace currently stated p-values with appropriate confidence intervals; (3) request isolation of the syntactic contribution by reporting standalone tree-LSTM performance, single-model fusion (concatenation/gating), and alternative ensembling strategies, plus analysis of per-example corrections to show whether tree-LSTM contributes systematic syntactic improvements rather than only variance reduction; (4) demand full reproducibility artifacts: public code repository with training scripts, seed values, exact preprocessing/tokenization, and model checkpoints or commands to reproduce reported numbers; (5) ask for a small systematic analysis (beyond anecdote) quantifying how often attention/gate patterns correspond to differing model decisions. Keep the editor's role central by soliciting these clarifying experiments and materials rather than substituting a final verdict on acceptability.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewer concerns, please (1) release the full code and exact data preprocessing scripts (including tokenization, casing, vocabulary/UNK handling) and provide commands to reproduce ESIM and HIM training and evaluation; (2) run and report ESIM, HIM, and key ablations across multiple random seeds (>=5), giving mean and standard deviation for train/dev/test accuracies and exact statistical-test details; (3) re-run or re-evaluate a small set of prior baselines within your codebase and preprocessing pipeline (or, if impossible, document differences precisely and estimate their likely impact) to support cross-paper comparisons; (4) report standalone performance of the tree-LSTM, results for alternative fusion strategies (representation concatenation, learned weighting, stacking), and per-example error attribution showing where tree-LSTM corrects ESIM errors; (5) expand interpretability analysis from a single anecdote to an aggregate study (e.g., sample N disagreements and quantify how often tree-LSTM attention/gate focus corresponds to correct vs incorrect labels); (6) fully disclose training protocol details omitted in the manuscript (number of epochs, early stopping policy, lr schedule, gradient clipping, random seeds) and provide model checkpoints or reproducible logs if feasible.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents ESIM, a modular enhanced sequential inference model (BiLSTM encoders, attention over contextualized hidden states, explicit local enhancement via concatenation/difference/product, BiLSTM inference composition, and average+max pooling) and an ensemble variant HIM that averages ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM. Within the authors' experimental pipeline ESIM is reported at 88.0% and HIM at 88.6% on SNLI. The paper includes targeted ablations attributing performance deltas to specific components and an illustrative interpretation example contrasting tree-LSTM and BiLSTM attention patterns. Overall contribution is engineering-focused: a carefully composed, well-documented architecture and empirical benchmarking with ablation analysis; however, important reproducibility and comparative-validation gaps remain that limit confidence in cross-paper superiority and in the isolated syntactic contribution.
strengths: Clear, modular architecture specification (equations and component descriptions for input encoding, local inference, inference composition, pooling) that supports reimplementation.
Targeted ablation experiments linking individual design choices (BiLSTM vs MLP, diff/prod enhancement, average+max vs summation pooling) to performance changes within the authors' pipeline.
Practical engineering contribution: a compact sequential model (ESIM) that, according to the manuscript, attains strong SNLI performance and can serve as a useful baseline.
Interpretability attempt: visualization (gate norms and attention) illustrating a case where tree-LSTM highlights constituency-level signals not emphasized by BiLSTM attention.
limitations: Comparative validity: main claims of outperforming prior work rely on published numbers (Table 1) rather than re-running key baselines (e.g., decomposable attention, prior LSTM/tree hybrids) under the exact preprocessing and training pipeline; small absolute gains (<=0.6%) are sensitive to preprocessing/tokenization differences (Assumption A1).

Statistical reporting: the manuscript asserts statistical significance (t-test p<0.01) for ablation differences but does not disclose number of independent runs, random seeds, per-run metrics, or standard deviations; without multi-seed means and variances, p-values and robustness of small deltas are unverifiable (Assumption A6).

Syntactic contribution ambiguity: the reported tree-based gain comes from ensembling ESIM with a tree-LSTM (averaging probabilities). Single-model tree-LSTM performance and alternative fusion strategies (feature fusion, learned weighting) are not clearly isolated, leaving open whether syntax provides intrinsic complementary signal or merely ensemble variance reduction (Assumptions A2, A4).

open_questions: Please report results averaged over multiple independent random seeds (recommend >=5): provide mean ± std for train/dev/test accuracies for ESIM, HIM, and each ablation, and state the exact statistical tests (paired/unpaired) used to compute p-values.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript introduces ESIM, a clearly defined sequential BiLSTM-based model with attention over contextualized hidden states, explicit local enhancement (concat, diff, product), BiLSTM inference composition, and average+max pooling, achieving reported 88.0% on SNLI. HIM ensembles ESIM with a syntactic tree-LSTM to reach 88.6%. Ablation experiments within the authors' pipeline link components to measured deltas, and an interpretability figure offers an illustrative example of syntactic vs sequential attention differences.

Strengths:
- Architecture is modular and well-specified with equations and clear component boundaries, facilitating reimplementation.
- Ablation table ties specific design choices (BiLSTM encodings, diff/prod features, pooling) to performance changes in the authors' experiments.
- Results indicate a strong practical baseline (ESIM) and suggest that syntax-aware models can provide modest complementary benefits when ensembled.

Limitations:
- Cross-paper comparison reliability: claimed wins over prior published models depend on published numbers rather than controlled re-runs under identical preprocessing; small gains (<=0.6%) are sensitive to such differences.
- Missing statistical detail: t-test claims lack disclosure of run counts, seeds, and standard deviations; single-run reporting prevents verifying robustness of small deltas.
- Ambiguous syntactic role: reported tree benefit comes via ensembling; standalone tree-LSTM effects and alternative fusion strategies are insufficiently reported to establish intrinsic syntactic value versus ensemble variance reduction.
- Reproducibility gaps: code link redacted, and critical training/protocol details (epochs, early stopping, seeds, exact preprocessing) are absent, hindering independent replication.

Open Questions:
- How do ESIM, HIM, and the ablated variants perform averaged over multiple independent runs (please provide mean ± std for ≥5 seeds) and what exact statistical tests are applied? 
- Can the authors re-run key baselines (e.g., decomposable attention of Parikh et al., 2016 and a notable LSTM/tree hybrid) under the identical preprocessing and training pipeline, or provide a concrete analysis quantifying how preprocessing differences might affect reported comparisons? 
- What is the standalone accuracy (with variance) of the syntactic tree-LSTM under the same training settings, and how do alternative fusion strategies (concatenation/gating, learned weighting, stacking) compare to simple probability averaging? 
- Can the authors make the full code, preprocessing scripts, seeds, and training scripts public (and ideally provide model checkpoints or training logs) so that reported numbers can be independently verified?

Transparency:
The manuscript is strong in describing architecture and many hyperparameters (optimizer, lr, batch size, dropout, embedding init, hidden dims) but omits seeds, number of epochs/early stopping rules, lr schedules, and the final code link is redacted. Statistical claims are stated without run-level variance data. Interpretability evidence is anecdotal. Releasing code and per-run logs plus controlled baseline re-runs would substantially improve transparency and the evidential basis for cross-paper claims.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects high trust in internally reported ablation patterns (authors ran controlled within-paper variants) but lower confidence in cross-paper superiority and robustness because of missing multi-seed reporting, redacted code, and lack of controlled baseline re-runs. If authors provide multi-seed averages and controlled baseline re-runs, uncertainty would narrow substantially.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Assessing the Ability of LSTMs to Learn Syntax-Sensitive Dependencies Tal Linzen1,2 Emmanuel Dupoux1 LSCP1 & IJN2, CNRS, EHESS and ENS, PSL Research University {tal.linzen, emmanuel.dupoux}@ens.fr Yoav Goldberg Computer Science Department Bar Ilan University yoav.goldberg@gmail.com Abstract The success of long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks in language process- ing is typically attributed to their ability to capture long-distance statistical regularities. Linguistic regularities are often sensitive to syntactic structure; can such dependencies be captured by LSTMs, which do not have ex- plicit structural representations? We begin ad- dressing this question using number agreement in English subject-verb dependencies. We probe the architecture’s grammatical compe- tence both using training objectives with an explicit grammatical target (number prediction, grammaticality judgments) and using language models. In the strongly supervised settings, the LSTM achieved very high overall accu- racy (less than 1% errors), but errors increased when sequential and structural information con- ﬂicted. The frequency of such errors rose sharply in the language-modeling setting. We conclude that LSTMs can capture a non-trivial amount of grammatical structure given targeted supervision, but stronger architectures may be required to further reduce errors; furthermore, the language modeling signal is insufﬁcient for capturing syntax-sensitive dependencies, and should be supplemented with more direct supervision if such dependencies need to be captured. 1 Introduction Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are highly effec- tive models of

Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Assessing the Ability of LSTMs to Learn Syntax-Sensitive Dependencies Tal Linzen1,2 Emmanuel Dupoux1 LSCP1 & IJN2, CNRS, EHESS and ENS, PSL Research University {tal.linzen, emmanuel.dupoux}@ens.fr Yoav Goldberg Computer Science Department Bar Ilan University yoav.goldberg@gmail.com Abstract The success of long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks in language process- ing is typically attributed to their ability to capture long-distance statistical regularities. Linguistic regularities are often sensitive to syntactic structure; can such dependencies be captured by LSTMs, which do not have ex- plicit structural representations? We begin ad- dressing this question using number agreement in English subject-verb dependencies. We probe the architecture’s grammatical compe- tence both using training objectives with an explicit grammatical target (number prediction, grammaticality judgments) and using language models. In the strongly supervised settings, the LSTM achieved very high overall accu- racy (less than 1% errors), but errors increased when sequential and structural information con- ﬂicted. The frequency of such errors rose sharply in the language-modeling setting.
